pos: n. (an idle talker; a scrap-gatherer of other men's words; rendering Greek spermologos and the Hebrew idiom “master of the tongue”)
etymology: From babble, an imitative word for confused speech, ultimately echoing Babel. The Greek spermologos is literally a seed-picker — the crow that hops about the market gathering scraps, then the man who gathers scraps of other men's learning and scatters them as his own.
biblical_def: The babbler is not merely a talkative man; he is a man whose speech has no root. Solomon sets him beside the serpent: “Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment; and a babbler is no better” (Ecc 10:11) — the charmer who speaks too late has lost his man, and the tongue that runs on without the fear of God bites the same way. The Athenian philosophers hurled the word at Paul on Mars' hill: “What will this babbler say?” (Act 17:18). They meant a seed-picker, a retailer of other men's scraps. The irony is total: the men who had spent their lives in nothing else but to tell or to hear some new thing called the one man in Athens with a word from God a babbler. Scripture therefore uses the term in two directions. Applied by the wise to the fool, it is a true judgment on speech without substance. Applied by the world to the preacher, it is the standing contempt of the natural man for the preaching of the cross, which is to the Greeks foolishness. The dictionary keeps both edges. A man must not be a babbler; and a man who preaches Christ must not be surprised when he is called one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a babbler as an idle talker; an irrational prattler; a teller of secrets; one who talks much and to little purpose.
webster_full: BABBLER, n. An idle talker; an irrational prattler; a teller of secrets.
2. One who talks much, and to little purpose; a great talker.
3. A telltale; one who cannot keep counsel, but publishes what should be concealed.
scriptures: Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment; and a babbler is no better.

Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection.
In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.
corruption_summary: The pulpit that gathers scraps — a story here, a study there, a line of verse, a clip of film — and scatters them for an hour without ever opening the text has become the seed-picker the Athenians thought Paul was.
corruption_paragraphs: Athens paid Paul the compliment of an insult. Spermologos was market slang for a bird that lives off dropped seed, and by extension for the man with no learning of his own who lives off fragments of everybody else's. What Athens did not see was that Paul had one thing to say and said it: Jesus, and the resurrection. The modern danger is the reverse of the ancient sneer. A great deal of contemporary preaching genuinely is scrap-gathering — an anecdote, a statistic, a quotation from a novelist, a felt need, a closing poem — assembled with real skill and containing no exposition of Scripture at all. That is babbling in Webster's exact sense: much talk to little purpose. The remedy is not fewer words but a rooted word. Paul at Athens quoted a pagan poet and named an unknown altar, and every borrowed scrap in that sermon was harnessed to one declared truth: God commandeth all men every where to repent, because he hath appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness. Scraps in the service of the resurrection are preaching; scraps in the service of nothing are babble.
roots_summary: Greek spermologos, seed-picker, scrap-gatherer (Act 17:18); Hebrew ba'al hallashon, master of the tongue (Ecc 10:11); compare Greek battologeo, to use vain repetitions (Mat 6:7).
roots_lines: Greek spermologos — literally seed-picker; a bird that scavenges the market, then a man who retails scraps of other men's learning; Acts 17:18.
Hebrew idiom ba'al hallashon — master, or owner, of the tongue; the man whose tongue owns him; Ecclesiastes 10:11.
Greek battologeo (G945) — to stammer, to heap up empty words; the Lord's own name for prayer that trusts in much speaking; Matthew 6:7.
usage: “A babbler is no better” — Solomon ranks the runaway tongue with the serpent that bites before the charmer speaks.
“What will this babbler say?” — Athens' verdict on the apostle, and the world's standing verdict on preaching.
“In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin” — the proverb that governs every pulpit and every dinner table.

pos: n. (violent disagreement; a standing apart into parties; rendering Greek stasis)
etymology: Latin dissensio, from dis-, apart, and sentire, to feel or think — to think apart. The Greek stasis is stronger still: a standing, a faction, and in Roman ears a riot.
biblical_def: Luke uses the word three times, and every use is instructive. At Antioch, false teachers came down from Judaea binding circumcision on the Gentiles, and “Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them” (Act 15:2). That dissension was not sin; it was the gospel refusing to be added to, and it drove the church to the Jerusalem council where the truth was settled in writing. In the Sanhedrin, Paul's confession of the resurrection produced a different sort: “there arose a dissension between the Pharisees and the Sadducees: and the multitude was divided” (Act 23:7), and it grew so violent that the chief captain feared Paul would be pulled in pieces (Act 23:10). Scripture therefore does not treat all division as evil. The word stasis can name a riot of the flesh or a stand for the faith. What decides is the thing stood for. Paul who stood against Peter to the face at Antioch is the same Paul who begs the Corinthians that there be no divisions among them. The rule is not peace at any price and not contention for its own sake, but truth held in love, and no small dissension when the gospel itself is at stake.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dissension as disagreement in opinion, usually a disagreement which produces warm debates or angry words; contention in words; strife; discord; quarrel; breach of friendship and union.
webster_full: DISSENSION, n. Disagreement in opinion, usually a disagreement which is violent, producing warm debates or angry words; contention in words; strife; discord; quarrel; breach of friendship and union.
2. Political or ecclesiastical faction; a standing apart into parties.
Debates, dissension, uproars are thy joy.
scriptures: Act 15:2

When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.
Act 23:7
And when he had so said, there arose a dissension between the Pharisees and the Sadducees: and the multitude was divided.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
corruption_summary: Dissension is now treated as the worst sin a church can commit, so that the man who contends for the faith is the offender and the man who corrupts it is the peacemaker.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct reads Acts 15:2 backwards. It sees Paul and Barnabas making no small dissension and concludes that Paul and Barnabas were the problem — that a humbler man would have absorbed the addition of circumcision for the sake of unity and spared the church a fight. Scripture judges otherwise: the Holy Ghost preserved that dissension in the record as the thing that produced the Jerusalem decree, and Galatians tells us plainly that giving place by subjection, no, not for an hour, was the only way the truth of the gospel might continue. The corruption is a counterfeit peace that treats every doctrinal contention as a failure of charity and every doctrinal surrender as maturity. It has a genuine mirror-image sin, and the dictionary names that too: the man who loves the fight, who finds a Sanhedrin in every congregation and calls his temper conviction. The test Scripture gives is the object. A dissension about the gospel is faithfulness; a dissension about preference, party, or personal standing is the flesh, and Paul calls it by that name in the list of Galatians 5:20.
roots_summary: Greek stasis (G4714), a standing, faction, insurrection, dissension; zetesis (G2214), questioning, debate; schisma (G4978), a rent or split, the word behind “divisions” in 1 Corinthians 1:10.
roots_lines: Greek stasis (G4714) — a standing, a faction, an insurrection; the same noun describes Barabbas' sedition and the Sanhedrin's uproar; Acts 15:2, 23:7, 23:10.
Greek zetesis (G2214) — questioning, debate, controversy; the companion word in Acts 15:2, translated “disputation”.
Greek schisma (G4978) — a tear, a rent, as in an unshrunk cloth on an old garment; the word Paul forbids in the church; 1 Corinthians 1:10, 11:18.
usage: “No small dissension and disputation” — the contention that produced the Jerusalem council and guarded the gospel of grace.
“There arose a dissension between the Pharisees and the Sadducees” — a council of the flesh dividing over a doctrine neither party held for God's sake.
“That there be no divisions among you” — the apostolic charge that binds every congregation not contending for the faith itself.

pos: n. pl. (contentions, quarrels, lawsuits; rendering Hebrew riyb and Greek machai)
etymology: From strive, Old French estriver, to contend. The Hebrew riyb is a legal word first — a suit, a controversy at law — before it is a brawl; the Greek machai are fights, and James asks whence they come.
biblical_def: David sings twice that the LORD “delivered me from the strivings of my people” (2Sa 22:44; Psa 18:43) — not from foreign armies but from the lawsuits, factions, and murmurings of Israel itself, and the deliverance made him head of the heathen. The most dangerous contention a servant of God faces is generally from within the covenant people. Paul gives Titus the church's rule: “avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain” (Tit 3:9). The strivings there are machai nomikai, fights about the law — endless disputes over pedigree, ceremony, and the fine print of ordinances, conducted by men who suppose gain is godliness. The verdict is not that the law is worthless but that these fights are: unprofitable, meaning they bear no fruit, and vain, meaning they lead nowhere. A servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient. That is not a call to indifference about doctrine; the same epistle commands Titus to rebuke sharply. It is a call to know the difference between a doctrine worth a council and a genealogy worth nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines striving as contention; contest; the act of making efforts in opposition; struggle; earnest endeavor.
webster_full: STRIVING, n. The act of contending; contest; contention; struggle for superiority.
2. Earnest endeavor; the act of making efforts to obtain or effect something.
STRIVE, v.i. To make efforts; to use exertions; also, to contend; to contest; to struggle in opposition.
scriptures: Thou also hast delivered me from the strivings of my people, thou hast kept me to be head of the heathen: a people which I knew not shall serve me.
Thou hast delivered me from the strivings of the people; and thou hast made me the head of the heathen: a people whom I have not known shall serve me.
Tit 3:9
But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
corruption_summary: The strivings Paul forbids have simply changed venue: the endless genealogies are now endless online controversies, conducted with the same heat and the same profitlessness, and mistaken for contending for the faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Titus 3:9 is one of the least obeyed verses in the New Testament among men who pride themselves on obeying Scripture. Paul names four things to avoid — foolish questions, genealogies, contentions, strivings about the law — and gives one reason: they are unprofitable and vain. He does not say they are false. Foolish questions can be perfectly accurate questions; a genealogy can be correct to the generation. The charge is that they bear no fruit. Whole ministries now exist on this diet: the daily controversy, the rebuttal of the rebuttal, the pedigree of who studied under whom, argued with real learning and producing nothing that could be called edification. Jude 3 commands us to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered, and the dictionary holds that command without flinching; but the faith once delivered is a short and glorious list, and most of what is contended for online is not on it. The test Paul gives is agricultural. After a year of it, what grew?
roots_summary: Hebrew riyb (H7379), strife, controversy, a suit at law; Greek mache (G3163), a fight or quarrel; Greek logomachia (G3055), a fight about words (1 Timothy 6:4).
roots_lines: Hebrew riyb (H7379) — strife, controversy, a legal cause; the same word names the LORD's controversy with His people in Micah 6:2; 2 Samuel 22:44, Psalm 18:43.
Greek mache (G3163) — a fight, a quarrel; always plural in the New Testament epistles and always condemned; Titus 3:9, 2 Timothy 2:23, James 4:1.
Greek logomachia (G3055) — a battle about words; Paul's diagnosis of the man proud, knowing nothing, doting about questions; 1 Timothy 6:4.
usage: “Delivered me from the strivings of my people” — David's hardest warfare was domestic.
“Strivings about the law…are unprofitable and vain” — the apostolic verdict on fruitless controversy.
“The servant of the Lord must not strive” — 2 Timothy 2:24, the same root, the same rule.

pos: v. (past tense of rail: to revile, to abuse with reproachful words; rendering Hebrew 'iyt and Greek blasphemeo)
etymology: Old French railler, to mock or banter, from a Latin root meaning to bray. In the Authorized Version the word has lost all lightness: to rail is to fly upon a man with the tongue.
biblical_def: Three scenes carry the word, and they climb. Nabal railed on David's young men when they asked bread in the name of the master who had been a wall unto his shepherds day and night (1Sa 25:14); the Hebrew is 'iyt, to swoop, the verb used of a bird of prey falling on the spoil. Then Calvary: “they that passed by railed on him, wagging their heads” (Mar 15:29), and the Greek is blasphemeo — the passers-by were not merely rude, they were blaspheming, and the Gospel writer says so. Finally one of the two malefactors, a dying man with nails in his own hands, “railed on him, saying, If thou be Christ, save thyself and us” (Luk 23:39). That is the terminal case of the sin: a man in the very act of perishing, hanging beside his only Savior, spending his last breath on abuse. The other thief heard the same words and answered, Dost not thou fear God? Railing is therefore not a small fault of manner. It is the tongue of the unbelieving heart under judgment, and Scripture sets it beside the tongue of the penitent thief for contrast in the same paragraph.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to rail as to utter reproaches; to scoff; to use insolent and reproachful language; to reproach or censure in opprobrious terms.
webster_full: RAIL, v.i. To utter reproaches; to scoff; to use insolent and reproachful language; to reproach or censure in opprobrious terms; followed by at or against.
And rail at arts he did not understand.
RAILED, pp. Reviled; reproached with harsh or contemptuous words.
scriptures: But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal's wife, saying, Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to salute our master; and he railed on them.
And they that passed by railed on him, wagging their heads, and saying, Ah, thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest it in three days,
And one of the malefactors which were hanged railed on him, saying, If thou be Christ, save thyself and us.
corruption_summary: Railing has been rehabilitated as courage: the man who is loudest in contempt is credited with boldness, and the apostolic ban on reviling is treated as a rule for the timid.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter set down the pattern in one clause: “who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1Pe 2:23). That is the Lord under the very railing of Mark 15:29, and it is offered not as an admirable temperament but as the example we are called to follow. Paul lists the railer among those with whom the church is not so much as to eat (1Co 5:11), and Jude marks it as the one thing Michael the archangel would not do even to the devil. The corruption is a public style, now common among professing Christians, in which contempt is the proof of conviction and mockery the proof of courage. It rewards the sharpest word rather than the truest one and calls the result boldness. Boldness in the New Testament is parrhesia, the freedom to say the whole truth plainly in the face of danger — Peter before the Sanhedrin, Paul before Agrippa — and not one syllable of it is contempt. A man may say the hardest thing in Scripture and never rail; a man may rail all day and never once say a hard thing that is true.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'iyt (H5860), to swoop or fly upon as a bird of prey; Greek blasphemeo (G987), to blaspheme, revile, defame; Greek loidoreo (G3058), to revile with abusive speech.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'iyt (H5860) — to rush or swoop upon, as a bird upon the carcases; used of Nabal's answer and of Israel flying upon the spoil; 1 Samuel 25:14, 15:19.
Greek blasphemeo (G987) — to speak injuriously, to blaspheme; the Spirit's own word for what the passers-by did at the cross; Mark 15:29, Luke 23:39.
Greek loidoreo (G3058) — to revile, to heap abuse; “when he was reviled, reviled not again”; 1 Peter 2:23, 1 Corinthians 4:12.
usage: “He railed on them” — Nabal answering kindness with contempt, and the churl's name became a proverb.
“They that passed by railed on him” — the crowd at Golgotha, blaspheming while they walked.
“One of the malefactors…railed on him” — the last words of a dying man spent on abuse.

pos: v. (past tense of contemn: to despise, to hold in contempt, to reject with scorn; rendering Hebrew bazah, na'ats, and buz)
etymology: Latin contemnere, to despise, from con- intensive and temnere, to slight. The Authorized Version keeps the strong Latin verb where modern speech has only the noun contempt.
biblical_def: The word marks a settled judgment of the heart, not a passing insult. In the portrait of the man who shall abide in God's tabernacle, it is a mark of righteousness: “In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD” (Psa 15:4). The godly man's esteem runs by God's valuation and not the world's: he will not flatter a wicked man because he is powerful, nor despise a poor saint because he is obscure. Turned the other way, it is the sin of the wilderness generation: “they rebelled against the words of God, and contemned the counsel of the most High” (Psa 107:11), and the bondage and irons of that psalm are the consequence. Solomon uses it for the world's bargain with love: “if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned” (Son 8:7) — the offer itself would be despised, because love is not purchasable. Isaiah uses it of Moab's glory brought to nothing (Isa 16:14). Contempt, then, is a real and sometimes righteous act of the soul. Everything depends on what is being weighed and by whose scales.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to contemn as to despise; to consider and treat as mean and despicable; to reject with disdain; to slight; to neglect as unworthy of regard.
webster_full: CONTEMN, v.t. To despise; to consider and treat as mean and despicable; to scorn.
2. To slight; to neglect as unworthy of regard; to reject with disdain.
CONTEMNED, pp. Despised; scorned; slighted; neglected; rejected with disdain.
scriptures: Psa 15:4
In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
Because they rebelled against the words of God, and contemned the counsel of the most High:
Son 8:7
Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.
corruption_summary: Psalm 15:4 is now read as a verse to be apologised for, because the modern conscience has been trained to believe that no man may be held in contempt for anything he does.
corruption_paragraphs: The fifteenth Psalm asks who shall abide in God's tabernacle and answers with a list of plain moral marks, one of which is that in his eyes a vile person is contemned. That clause is a genuine embarrassment to the modern conscience, and it is regularly softened into meaning nothing more than mild disapproval. Scripture means what it says: the man who walks with God does not honour wickedness, does not court it, does not seek the friendship of the vile because the vile is useful to him. And the psalm is careful to give the other half in the same breath — he honoureth them that fear the LORD. It is a matched pair, and both halves are about the same thing: whose estimate of a man do you take, God's or the world's? The corruption is not that people have grown too kind. It is that the valuation has been inverted. The same age that cannot bear to contemn a vile person has no difficulty at all contemning them that fear the LORD, and does it daily. Psalm 15 was never an invitation to be harsh. It was an invitation to weigh men on the only scales that will still be standing at the judgment.
roots_summary: Hebrew bazah (H959), to despise, to hold in contempt; na'ats (H5006), to spurn or reject with contempt; buz (H936), to hold in derision.
roots_lines: Hebrew bazah (H959) — to despise, to show contempt for; the same verb says of Christ that He was despised and rejected of men; Psalm 15:4, Isaiah 53:3.
Hebrew na'ats (H5006) — to spurn, to reject, to blaspheme; the wilderness sin against the counsel of the most High; Psalm 107:11, Numbers 14:11.
Hebrew buz (H936) — to hold in derision; the world's verdict on the man who would buy love with substance; Song of Solomon 8:7, Proverbs 6:30.
usage: “In whose eyes a vile person is contemned” — the man who values by God's scales and not the world's.
“Contemned the counsel of the most High” — the wilderness sin, and the irons that followed it.
“It would utterly be contemned” — love refuses to be bought, and despises the offer.

pos: v. (to challenge to combat; to reproach or taunt an enemy; rendering Hebrew za'am and charaph)
etymology: Old French desfier, to renounce faith or allegiance, from Latin dis- and fidere, to trust. To defy is first to break off trust, and then to challenge.
biblical_def: Balak hired Balaam with a single commission: “Come, curse me Jacob, and come, defy Israel” (Num 23:7), and the prophet had to answer, “How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed? or how shall I defy, whom the LORD hath not defied?” (Num 23:8). The whole doctrine of Israel's security is in that reply: no hired tongue can defy what God has blessed. The word's second and greater theatre is the valley of Elah, where the Philistine said, “I defy the armies of Israel this day” (1Sa 17:10), and the men of Israel could only report that he had come up to defy Israel (1Sa 17:25). It was David who alone heard the challenge correctly: “who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?” (1Sa 17:26). Saul heard a giant defying soldiers; David heard a creature defying the living God, and that hearing is the whole difference between the army that trembled and the boy who ran toward the champion. Defiance in Scripture is thus never finally aimed at men. It is aimed at the God whose name they bear, and it is answered by Him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to defy as to dare; to provoke to combat or strife; to challenge; to brave; to treat with contempt; to slight or set at nought.
webster_full: DEFY, v.t. To dare; to provoke to combat or strife, by appealing to the courage of another; to invite one to contest; to challenge.
2. To dare; to brave; to offer to hazard a conflict by manifesting a contempt of opposition, attack or hostile force.
3. To challenge to say or do any thing; to treat with contempt or despise.
scriptures: Num 23:8
How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed? or how shall I defy, whom the LORD hath not defied?
And the Philistine said, I defy the armies of Israel this day; give me a man, that we may fight together.

And David spake to the men that stood by him, saying, What shall be done to the man that killeth this Philistine, and taketh away the reproach from Israel? for who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?
corruption_summary: Goliath has been reduced to a metaphor for personal obstacles — the giant of debt, the giant of fear — which quietly relocates the story from the honour of God to the improvement of the hearer.
corruption_paragraphs: David's question in 1 Samuel 17:26 is the hinge of the chapter, and it is the line most often left out of the retelling. The popular treatment of the passage makes the giant a symbol of whatever is currently large in the listener's life and makes David a model of self-confidence, five smooth stones and all. What the text actually reports is a boy who was indignant for a name. The armies of Israel had heard Goliath forty days and heard only a threat; David heard a blasphemy. His courage was not a character trait he brought to the valley; it was the necessary consequence of hearing the challenge rightly. That is why the same chapter has him say that the battle is the LORD's, and He will give you into our hands. Where the sermon relocates the story into the hearer's ambitions, it has to supply the confidence from somewhere else — usually from the hearer — and the result is a message about self-belief preached from a text about the honour of God. Balaam's answer is the antidote: no man defies whom the LORD has not defied, and no man is defied whom the LORD defends.
roots_summary: Hebrew za'am (H2194), to be indignant, to denounce or curse; charaph (H2778), to reproach, taunt, defy; qalas (H7046), to scoff at.
roots_lines: Hebrew za'am (H2194) — to be indignant, to rage, to denounce; Balaam's commission and his refusal; Numbers 23:7-8.
Hebrew charaph (H2778) — to reproach, to taunt, to expose to scorn; the champion's standing challenge in the valley of Elah; 1 Samuel 17:10, 17:26, 17:45.
Hebrew qalas (H7046) — to scoff, to mock; the companion sin of the taunting tongue; 2 Kings 2:23, Ezekiel 16:31.
usage: “How shall I defy, whom the LORD hath not defied?” — a hired prophet discovering the limits of his trade.
“I defy the armies of Israel this day” — the challenge that stood forty days unanswered.
“That he should defy the armies of the living God” — David hearing the blasphemy the whole camp had missed.

pos: v. (to affirm solemnly; to testify before witnesses; to declare with a warning; rendering Hebrew 'uwd)
etymology: Latin protestari, from pro-, before, and testari, to witness — to testify publicly, in the face of all. The modern sense of objection is a narrowing; the Authorized Version keeps the original breadth.
biblical_def: To protest in the Authorized Version is not to complain but to swear a thing publicly. Judah reports to Jacob that “the man did solemnly protest unto us, saying, Ye shall not see my face, except your brother be with you” (Gen 43:3) — Joseph had put the family under a formal declaration. When Israel demanded a king, the LORD told Samuel to give them their way and then to warn them of the cost: “protest solemnly unto them, and shew them the manner of the king that shall reign over them” (1Sa 8:9). The Hebrew is 'uwd, to testify, to call witnesses, to bear solemn warning — the same root that stands behind the word testimony. Paul takes it up in a great oath of the Christian life: “I protest by your rejoicing which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die daily” (1Co 15:31), swearing by the joy he had in the church he had begotten that his life was a continual dying. The biblical protest is therefore an oath before God, and the word carries the weight of court and covenant. It is the language of the herald, not of the malcontent. The name Protestant was earned in that older sense: not men who complained, but men who testified.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to protest as to affirm with solemnity; to make a solemn declaration of a fact or opinion; and, of a witness, to declare formally in the face of others.
webster_full: PROTEST, v.i. To affirm with solemnity; to make a solemn declaration of a fact or opinion.
PROTEST, v.t. To call to witness; to invoke as a witness; also, to prove; to show; to give evidence of.
PROTEST, n. A solemn declaration of opinion, commonly against some act; a formal and public declaration.
scriptures: Gen 43:3
And Judah spake unto him, saying, The man did solemnly protest unto us, saying, Ye shall not see my face, except your brother be with you.
Now therefore hearken unto their voice: howbeit yet protest solemnly unto them, and shew them the manner of the king that shall reign over them.
I protest by your rejoicing which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die daily.
corruption_summary: Protest has been emptied of oath and narrowed to grievance, so that the word which once meant to testify for something now means only to be against something.
corruption_paragraphs: The English word has travelled a long way downhill. In 1529 the German princes at Speyer entered a protestatio — a formal legal testimony that they could not, before God and conscience, consent to the revocation of the gospel's liberty — and the name Protestant was fastened on the churches of the Reformation from that act. It was a positive word. They were testifying to something: justification by faith alone, the sole authority of Scripture, the crown rights of Christ over His church. Modern usage has reduced protest to the noise a crowd makes when displeased, and the reduction has quietly reshaped how many Protestants understand themselves — as a movement defined by what it left rather than by what it confessed. The corruption is worth naming precisely because it disarms. A church that knows it is protesting for the finished work of Christ has something to say on any day of the week; a church that knows only that it is against Rome has nothing to say once Rome is out of the news. Samuel's protest to Israel is the model: he warned them of the king, and he did it by shewing them the truth.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'uwd (H5749), to testify, to bear witness, to warn solemnly; Greek ne (G3513), a particle of strong affirmation, “by” in an oath (1 Corinthians 15:31); compare diamarturomai (G1263), to charge earnestly.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'uwd (H5749) — to testify, to admonish, to warn solemnly; the root behind 'eduth, testimony, the name of the ark's tables; Genesis 43:3, 1 Samuel 8:9.
Greek ne (G3513) — the particle of solemn affirmation, used only once in the New Testament, in Paul's oath by the rejoicing of the Corinthians; 1 Corinthians 15:31.
Greek diamarturomai (G1263) — to testify thoroughly, to charge before God; Paul's word for his own ministry of warning; Acts 20:21, 2 Timothy 4:1.
usage: “The man did solemnly protest unto us” — Joseph binding his brothers by a public declaration.
“Protest solemnly unto them, and shew them the manner of the king” — the warning that came with the granted request.
“I protest…I die daily” — Paul's oath on the life of an apostle.

pos: adv. (disgracefully; with insult and dishonour; rendering Hebrew bosh and Greek atimazo and hubrizo)
etymology: Old English scamu, shame, with the adverbial ending. The Greek hubrizo behind 1 Thessalonians 2:2 gives us hubris: to treat a man with insolent outrage.
biblical_def: Hosea uses the word of Israel herself: “their mother hath played the harlot: she that conceived them hath done shamefully” (Hos 2:5), and the shame is not embarrassment but covenant adultery — going after lovers who she supposed gave her bread and water, wool and flax. In the parable of the vineyard the word describes what tenants do to a lord's messengers: they cast stones at one and “sent him away shamefully handled” (Mar 12:4), and Luke's parallel says they “entreated him shamefully, and sent him away empty” (Luk 20:11). This is the settled treatment of the prophets, and the parable is heading somewhere: last of all he sent unto them his son. Paul then applies the same verb to his own ministry: “after that we had suffered before, and were shamefully entreated, as ye know, at Philippi, we were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God with much contention” (1Th 2:2). The Greek there is hubrizo — the beating and the inner prison and the stocks, done to a Roman citizen without trial. Paul mentions it not to be pitied but to prove a point: shameful handling did not stop the message, and the Thessalonians had the gospel because it did not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shamefully as disgracefully; in a manner to bring reproach; with indignity; and, in an older use, infamously.
webster_full: SHAMEFULLY, adv. Disgracefully; in a manner to bring reproach.
2. With indignity or indecency; in a manner that may cause shame.
SHAMEFUL, a. That brings shame or disgrace; scandalous; disgraceful; injurious to reputation.
scriptures: Hos 2:5

For their mother hath played the harlot: she that conceived them hath done shamefully: for she said, I will go after my lovers, that give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, mine oil and my drink.
And again he sent another servant: and they beat him also, and entreated him shamefully, and sent him away empty.
But even after that we had suffered before, and were shamefully entreated, as ye know, at Philippi, we were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God with much contention.
corruption_summary: Shame is now treated as a purely social injury to be dismantled, so that the biblical distinction between the shame a man ought to feel for sin and the shame unjustly heaped on him for righteousness is lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture knows three shames and keeps them apart. There is the shame that belongs to sin and ought to be felt — Hosea's Israel has done shamefully, and Jeremiah's complaint against his generation is that they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush. There is the shame unjustly inflicted on the faithful — Paul shamefully entreated at Philippi, the servants of the vineyard sent away empty. And there is the shame Christ despised on the cross, borne for others. The modern account collapses all three into one category to be eliminated, on the assumption that shame as such is an injury done by society to the self. The result is that a man who ought to be ashamed is taught that his shame is a wound inflicted on him, while a church shamefully entreated for the gospel is taught to regard the treatment as a failure of its own public relations. Paul's response at Thessalonica is the corrective, and it is entirely unsentimental: we were shamefully entreated, and we were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God. The shame was real, it was unjust, and it changed nothing about the errand.
roots_summary: Hebrew bosh (H954), to be ashamed, to be confounded; Greek atimazo (G818), to dishonour, to treat with contempt; Greek hubrizo (G5195), to treat insolently, to outrage.
roots_lines: Hebrew bosh (H954) — to be ashamed, confounded, disappointed; the covenant word for Israel's harlotry and for the hope that never fails; Hosea 2:5, Psalm 25:3.
Greek atimazo (G818) — to dishonour, to treat as without honour; the vineyard servants and the apostles counted worthy to suffer it; Mark 12:4, Acts 5:41.
Greek hubrizo (G5195) — to treat with insolent outrage; the beating and stocks at Philippi, and the Lord's own foretelling of His passion; 1 Thessalonians 2:2, Luke 18:32.
usage: “She that conceived them hath done shamefully” — the shame that belongs to covenant unfaithfulness.
“Entreated him shamefully, and sent him away empty” — the standing treatment of the prophets, and the parable's warning.
“Shamefully entreated…we were bold in our God” — Philippi did not silence Thessalonica.

pos: n. and part. (reasoning, debating, contending in argument; rendering Greek suzeteo, zetesis, and dialegomai)
etymology: Latin disputare, from dis-, apart, and putare, to reckon — to reckon a matter out. The Authorized Version uses the word both for holy reasoning from the Scriptures and for the wrangling of hardened men.
biblical_def: Luke reports both kinds within a few chapters. The synagogue of the Libertines rose up “disputing with Stephen” (Act 6:9), and when they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake they suborned false witnesses instead — disputing that ends in murder because it never intended to be persuaded. At Jerusalem, “when there had been much disputing, Peter rose up” (Act 15:7), and the disputing was the honest labour of a council that then reached a settled judgment. At Ephesus Paul went into the synagogue and spake boldly for three months, “disputing and persuading the things concerning the kingdom of God” (Act 19:8), and when divers were hardened he separated the disciples and continued “disputing daily in the school of one Tyrannus” (Act 19:9). The Greek there is dialegomai — to reason through a matter — and Luke plainly counts it apostolic work. Two years of daily reasoning is how all Asia heard the word. The dictionary therefore refuses to make argument itself the villain. Paul reasoned; Stephen reasoned; the council reasoned. What Scripture condemns is the disputing that has already decided, and the disputing about nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines disputing as the act of contending in argument; controversy in words; the reasoning or arguing of contending parties.
webster_full: DISPUTING, ppr. Contending by words or arguments; controverting; debating.
DISPUTING, n. The act of contending in words; controversy; altercation.
DISPUTE, v.i. To contend in argument; to reason or argue in opposition; to debate; to alter cate.
scriptures: Act 6:9
Then there arose certain of the synagogue, which is called the synagogue of the Libertines, and Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and of them of Cilicia and of Asia, disputing with Stephen.
Act 19:8
And he went into the synagogue, and spake boldly for the space of three months, disputing and persuading the things concerning the kingdom of God.
Php 2:14
Do all things without murmurings and disputings:
corruption_summary: Two errors stand on either side of this word: the church that will not reason at all because argument feels unkind, and the church that reasons ceaselessly and never arrives at a judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: A common modern instinct treats all argument as a failure of love, and quotes Philippians 2:14 — do all things without murmurings and disputings — to close every doctrinal question before it opens. But Paul who wrote that verse is the same Paul who disputed daily for two years in the school of Tyrannus, and Philippians 2:14 is about the grumbling of a congregation with one another, not about reasoning from the Scriptures with the lost. The opposite error is just as real and rather more common among those most careful about doctrine: a disputing that never terminates. Acts 15 shows the pattern Scripture blesses. There was much disputing, and then Peter rose up, and then James gave sentence, and then the church wrote it down and sent it out. Debate served a decision. The corruption is debate as a permanent condition — the conference, the podcast, the endless thread, in which no question is ever closed because closing it would end the discussion, and the discussion has become the product. Paul reasoned in order to persuade. The measure of his disputing was in Acts 19:10: all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus.
roots_summary: Greek suzeteo (G4802), to search together, to dispute; zetesis (G2214), a questioning or debate; dialegomai (G1256), to reason through, to discourse; dialogismos (G1261), inward reasoning or murmuring.
roots_lines: Greek suzeteo (G4802) — to search or reason together, and so to dispute; the synagogue against Stephen, and the scribes against the disciples; Acts 6:9, Mark 9:14.
Greek dialegomai (G1256) — to reason, to discourse, to argue a case; Paul's regular method in synagogue and school; Acts 17:2, 19:8-9.
Greek dialogismos (G1261) — reasonings, disputings of the heart; the murmuring Paul forbids the church; Philippians 2:14, Romans 14:1.
usage: “Disputing with Stephen” — argument that could not resist the wisdom, and turned to false witnesses.
“Disputing and persuading the things concerning the kingdom of God” — the apostolic pattern; reasoning aimed at persuasion.
“Do all things without murmurings and disputings” — the congregational rule, not a ban on reasoning.

pos: v. (third person singular of boast: to vaunt, to glory in self; rendering Hebrew halal and Greek aucheo)
etymology: Middle English bosten, of uncertain origin, to brag. The Hebrew halal is the same root as hallelujah: to shine, to make a noise of praise. Boasting is praise pointed at the wrong object.
biblical_def: That the Hebrew for boasting is the root of hallelujah is the whole doctrine in one word. Man was made to make a shining noise about something; the only question is what. “The wicked boasteth of his heart's desire, and blesseth the covetous, whom the LORD abhorreth” (Psa 10:3) — here the praise is aimed at appetite, and the man blesses the very greed God abhors. Solomon shows the merchant's version: “It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasteth” (Pro 20:14) — he ran the goods down to get the price, then bragged of the bargain, and the two halves of that verse are one dishonest man. Again: “Whoso boasteth himself of a false gift is like clouds and wind without rain” (Pro 25:14), the promise of refreshment that delivers none. James brings it to the tongue itself: “the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!” (Jas 3:5). Over against all of it stands Jeremiah's rule, quoted twice by Paul: let him that glorieth glory in the Lord. The mouth is not to be silenced but redirected.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to boast as to brag or vaunt one's self; to glory; to speak ostentatiously; to display in ostentatious language.
webster_full: BOAST, v.i. To brag, or vaunt one's self; to make an ostentatious display, in speech, of one's own worth, property, or actions.
2. To glory; to speak with laudable pride and exultation of meritorious persons or things.
BOASTETH. Third person singular of boast; vaunteth; glorieth.
scriptures: Psa 10:3
For the wicked boasteth of his heart's desire, and blesseth the covetous, whom the LORD abhorreth.
Whoso boasteth himself of a false gift is like clouds and wind without rain.
Jas 3:5
Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!
corruption_summary: Boasting has been rebranded as personal branding, and the man who advertises himself continually is not thought proud but professional.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 25:14 is a picture drawn for a farming country in a dry land: clouds pile up, wind rises, everyone looks to the sky — and nothing falls. That is the man who boasts of a gift he has not given. The modern form of this is not usually a lie about a specific gift; it is a whole manner of public life in which a man is continually announcing his own worth as the ordinary condition of doing business. The vocabulary has been made respectable — profile, platform, brand, presence — and it is now genuinely difficult to distinguish honest testimony to what God has done from advertisement of what one has done, because the two are said in the same words on the same page. Scripture's test is not volume but object, and it is a knife: he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. Paul boasted freely, and the things he chose were his chains, his stripes, his thorn, and the churches Christ built through him. A man may test his own speech by asking what, in the last month, he actually made a shining noise about. That is what he worships.
roots_summary: Hebrew halal (H1984), to shine, to praise, to boast — the root of hallelujah; Greek aucheo / megalaucheo (G3166), to speak great things; Greek kauchaomai (G2744), to glory or boast.
roots_lines: Hebrew halal (H1984) — to shine, to make a noise of praise, and so to boast; the root of hallelujah, praise ye the LORD; Psalm 10:3, Psalm 34:2, Jeremiah 9:24.
Greek megalaucheo / aucheo (G3166) — to speak great things, to talk big; James' verdict on the tongue; James 3:5.
Greek kauchaomai (G2744) — to glory, to boast; used positively of glorying in the Lord and in tribulations; Romans 5:3, 1 Corinthians 1:31, Galatians 6:14.
usage: “The wicked boasteth of his heart's desire” — praise aimed at appetite.
“Clouds and wind without rain” — the promise of a gift never given.
“The tongue…boasteth great things” — a little member and a great fire.

pos: v. (third person singular of flatter: to praise falsely for advantage; to make smooth with the tongue; rendering Hebrew chalaq)
etymology: Old French flater, to stroke or smooth with the hand. The Hebrew chalaq means to be smooth, to divide, to apportion — a smooth tongue and a divided heart are the same word.
biblical_def: Flattery in Scripture is a weapon, and Proverbs treats it as one. It begins at home: “he flattereth himself in his own eyes, until his iniquity be found to be hateful” (Psa 36:2). Self-flattery is the first and most successful lie a man tells, and it works precisely by keeping the sin from ever looking hateful to him. Then the strange woman, twice: Wisdom is given to deliver thee from “the stranger which flattereth with her words” (Pro 2:16; Pro 7:5). Then the talebearer: “meddle not with him that flattereth with his lips” (Pro 20:19) — the man who is warm to your face collects secrets to spend elsewhere. Then the great reversal: “He that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour than he that flattereth with the tongue” (Pro 28:23). The rebuke wins in the end; the flattery only wins now. And the plainest of all: “A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet” (Pro 29:5). Flattery is not excessive kindness. It is trapping, and Solomon calls it a net. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to flatter as to please by artful commendation or compliments; to gratify self-love by praise or obsequiousness; to encourage by favorable notice.
webster_full: FLATTER, v.t. To please by artful commendation or compliments; to gratify self-love; to sooth by praise.
2. To please; to gratify; as, to flatter one's vanity or pride.
3. To raise false hopes in, by praise or representation; to encourage by favorable notice.
scriptures: Psa 36:2
For he flattereth himself in his own eyes, until his iniquity be found to be hateful.
He that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour than he that flattereth with the tongue.
Pro 29:5
A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet.
corruption_summary: Flattery has become the ordinary register of encouragement, and a generation taught to affirm everything has lost the faithful wound of a friend.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 29:5 is one of the most counter-cultural verses in the book because it classifies flattery not as excessive niceness but as trapping: a man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet. The net is the point. Flattery works by telling a man what he wants to hear until he walks confidently into ground he would have avoided had anyone told him the truth. A whole vocabulary of affirmation now stands ready for this purpose, and it is genuinely difficult to tell encouragement from flattery by the words alone, because they are frequently the same words. Scripture gives the test in the next verse-pair rather than in the vocabulary: he that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour. Encouragement is willing to say the hard thing and takes the short-term cost; flattery is not and does not. The pastoral loss is severe. A church in which no one has ever been told a difficult truth about himself has no friends in it in the biblical sense, only well-wishers — and Psalm 36:2 warns that the man nobody will correct will finish the job himself, flattering himself in his own eyes until his iniquity is past finding hateful.
roots_summary: Hebrew chalaq (H2505), to be smooth, to divide, to flatter; cheleq, smoothness of speech; Greek kolakeia (G2850), flattering words, used of Paul's refusal in 1 Thessalonians 2:5.
roots_lines: Hebrew chalaq (H2505) — to be smooth, and so to divide or apportion; the smooth tongue and the divided heart share one root; Psalm 36:2, Proverbs 2:16, 28:23.
Hebrew chelqah — smoothness, a smooth place; Jacob's neck was smooth, and so is the strange woman's mouth; Proverbs 5:3, Genesis 27:16.
Greek kolakeia (G2850) — flattery, flattering speech used as a cloak of covetousness; Paul denies ever using it; 1 Thessalonians 2:5.
usage: “He flattereth himself in his own eyes” — the first and most successful lie.
“More favour than he that flattereth with the tongue” — the rebuke wins in the end.
“Spreadeth a net for his feet” — flattery classified as trapping.

pos: v. (third person singular of testify: to bear witness, to affirm as an eyewitness; rendering Greek martureo)
etymology: Latin testificari, from testis, a witness. The Greek martureo gives English martyr: the witness who seals his testimony with his blood.
biblical_def: The word runs from indictment to benediction. Hosea: “the pride of Israel testifieth to his face” (Hos 7:10) — a man's own pride is a witness against him in court, and needs no other accuser. John the Baptist of Christ: “what he hath seen and heard, that he testifieth; and no man receiveth his testimony” (Joh 3:32) — the perfect Witness, reporting the Father's house from firsthand sight, and the world declining the evidence. John of himself at the close of the Gospel: “This is the disciple which testifieth of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true” (Joh 21:24) — the apostolic claim to eyewitness authority on which the canon rests. The writer to the Hebrews of the Son's priesthood: “For he testifieth, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec” (Heb 7:17), where the Scripture itself is the one testifying. And at the end of the Book: “He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly” (Rev 22:20). Christianity is not a philosophy deduced; it is a testimony borne. That is why its central verb is a courtroom verb, and why its witnesses were prepared to die rather than amend the record.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to testify as to make a solemn declaration, verbal or written, to establish a fact; to bear witness; to affirm or declare solemnly.
webster_full: TESTIFY, v.i. To make a solemn declaration, verbal or written, to establish some fact; to give testimony for the purpose of communicating to others a knowledge of something not known to them.
2. In Scripture, to affirm or declare solemnly.
TESTIFY, v.t. To bear witness to; to support the truth of by testimony; to affirm or declare.
scriptures: Joh 3:32
And what he hath seen and heard, that he testifieth; and no man receiveth his testimony.
This is the disciple which testifieth of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true.
He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus.
corruption_summary: Testimony has been reduced to a report of private feeling, so that what a Christian testifies to is his own inner experience rather than a public fact he has seen.
corruption_paragraphs: John 21:24 is the seal on a book: this is the disciple which testifieth of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true. The claim is evidentiary. A man saw the risen Christ, ate broiled fish with Him by the sea of Tiberias, and wrote it down, and the church certifies the witness. That is what the New Testament means by testimony — the same word a Roman court would use, and the same standard: what a witness saw and heard. The modern church has largely reassigned the word to the interior life. A testimony has come to mean the story of how one came to feel about God as one now feels, which is not nothing but is not what martureo means and cannot bear the weight the New Testament puts on it. The two are easily distinguished by a question: if the witness is mistaken about his own feelings, someone is disappointed; if he is mistaken about the empty tomb, the whole faith is vain and we are found false witnesses of God. Paul says exactly that in 1 Corinthians 15. Christian testimony stakes itself on facts outside the witness, which is precisely why it was worth dying for.
roots_summary: Greek martureo (G3140), to bear witness, to testify; marturia (G3141), the testimony borne; martus (G3144), a witness, and so a martyr.
roots_lines: Greek martureo (G3140) — to bear witness, to affirm what one has seen and heard; John 3:32, 21:24, Revelation 22:20.
Greek marturia (G3141) — the testimony itself; the Spirit, the water, and the blood bear witness, and the witness of God is greater than that of men; 1 John 5:9.
Greek martus (G3144) — a witness; Stephen is called the Lord's martus and the word passed into English as martyr; Acts 22:20, Hebrews 12:1.
usage: “What he hath seen and heard, that he testifieth” — the perfect Witness reporting the Father.
“We know that his testimony is true” — the church's certificate on the eyewitness.
“He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly” — the last testimony in the canon.

pos: v. (third person singular of deny: to disown, to refuse to confess; rendering Greek arneomai)
etymology: Old French denier, from Latin denegare, to refuse or say no. The Greek arneomai is the verb of Peter in the high priest's hall and of the apostate in John's epistle: to disown a person one is known to belong to.
biblical_def: Denial in the New Testament is not primarily the rejection of a proposition; it is the disowning of a Person. The Lord states the reciprocity plainly: “he that denieth me before men shall be denied before the angels of God” (Luk 12:9). John then applies the test to doctrine: “Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son” (1Jn 2:22). The two denials are one act, because the Father is not known apart from the Son — whosoever denieth the Son, the same hath not the Father (1Jn 2:23). This is the sharpest boundary the New Testament draws, and it cuts through every proposal of a shared worship of one God across the Christian and non-Christian confessions: a religion that denies the Son does not thereby retain the Father. Yet the same Scripture that sets the boundary shows a man crossing back. Peter denied his Lord three times with oaths and curses, and was restored by the sea with a threefold charge to feed the sheep, and is writing epistles by 1 Peter 1. Denial is deadly; it is not, while there is breath and repentance, final.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to deny as to contradict; to declare a statement untrue; to refuse to grant; to disown; to refuse to acknowledge; to renounce.
webster_full: DENY, v.t. To contradict; to gainsay; to declare a statement or position not to be true.
2. To refuse to grant; as, we asked for bread, and the man denied us.
3. To disown; to refuse or neglect to acknowledge; not to confess.
scriptures: Luk 12:9
But he that denieth me before men shall be denied before the angels of God.
Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son.
If we suffer, we shall also reign with him: if we deny him, he also will deny us:
corruption_summary: The most common form of denial today is not a stated rejection of Christ but a quiet omission of Him — a God-language kept and a Son-clause dropped — and 1 John 2:23 names that arrangement precisely.
corruption_paragraphs: First John 2:23 is the verse that will not permit a common theism. Whosoever denieth the Son, the same hath not the Father. It is not a claim that other religions are wicked in every part or that their adherents are insincere; it is a claim about who the Father is, namely, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the Father cannot be had by anyone who will not have the Son. John writes this as a test of spirits within the church, against men who had gone out from us because they were not of us, and his standard is confession of the incarnate Christ. The corruption in our day rarely announces itself as denial. It appears as omission: public prayer to a God with no Son named, statements of shared faith in which the offensive clause is left out for the sake of the platform, ministries that will speak of God, values, and purpose for years without confessing that Jesus is the Christ. Christ's own word in Luke 12:9 covers the omission as surely as the denial, because the standard is confession before men. The measure is not what a man privately holds but what he is willing to be known for.
roots_summary: Greek arneomai (G720), to deny, disown, refuse, reject; aparneomai (G533), to deny utterly, used of Peter and of self-denial; homologeo (G3670), to confess, its opposite.
roots_lines: Greek arneomai (G720) — to deny, to disown, to refuse to acknowledge; used of Peter, of the antichrist, and of the servant who denies his Master; Luke 12:9, 1 John 2:22, 2 Timothy 2:12.
Greek aparneomai (G533) — to deny utterly; the Lord's word both for Peter's coming denial and for the disciple who must deny himself; Mark 8:34, Mark 14:30.
Greek homologeo (G3670) — to say the same thing, to confess; the exact opposite of denial and the mark of salvation; Romans 10:9, 1 John 4:15.
usage: “He that denieth me before men shall be denied before the angels of God” — the reciprocity Christ states without softening.
“He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son” — John's test of spirits.
“If we deny him, he also will deny us” — the faithful saying, set beside the promise that He abideth faithful.

pos: v. (third person singular of prophesy: to speak forth the word of God; rendering Hebrew naba' and Greek propheteuo)
etymology: Greek propheteuo, from pro-, forth or before, and phemi, to speak — to speak forth. The prophet is first a mouth for God and only secondarily a foreteller.
biblical_def: Jeremiah gives the test that governs the office: “The prophet which prophesieth of peace, when the word of the prophet shall come to pass, then shall the prophet be known, that the LORD hath truly sent him” (Jer 28:9). A prophecy of peace is the easy word, the popular word, and the one Hananiah had just given; the burden of proof lies on the comfortable prophet, and time is the examiner. Ezekiel meets the opposite evasion: the house of Israel says “the vision that he seeth is for many days to come, and he prophesieth of the times that are far off” (Eze 12:27) — conceding that the word is true while pushing its fulfilment beyond the reach of repentance. Zechariah records the day when a father and mother would themselves execute a lying prophet from their own house (Zec 13:3). In the New Testament the word turns pastoral: “he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort” (1Co 14:3), and prophesying is preferred above tongues precisely because it builds the church rather than the speaker: “he that prophesieth edifieth the church” (1Co 14:4). The canon being closed, the dictionary holds the cessationist position: what remains is the ministry that Corinthians describes — the church built up by the plain declaration of God's already-given word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to prophesy as to foretell future events; to predict; and, in Scripture use, to utter predictions and to preach; to instruct in religious doctrine.
webster_full: PROPHESY, v.t. To foretell future events; to predict.
2. To foreshow.
PROPHESY, v.i. To utter predictions; to make declaration of events to come. In Scripture, to preach; to instruct in religious doctrine; to interpret or explain Scripture or religious subjects.
scriptures: Jer 28:9
The prophet which prophesieth of peace, when the word of the prophet shall come to pass, then shall the prophet be known, that the LORD hath truly sent him.
Son of man, behold, they of the house of Israel say, The vision that he seeth is for many days to come, and he prophesieth of the times that are far off.
But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort.
corruption_summary: The modern prophetic movement has restored the title without the test: men prophesy of peace and prosperity, and Jeremiah's standard of fulfilment is never applied to a word that fails.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 28 is the chapter the contemporary prophetic movement has to answer, and it is short enough to read in a minute. Hananiah prophesied peace — within two full years the vessels return, the king comes home — and he did it in the name of the LORD of hosts, publicly, in the house of the LORD, before all the people. Jeremiah's reply is the rule of verse 9: the prophet of peace is proved by fulfilment, and Deuteronomy 18:22 had already fixed the penalty for failure. Hananiah died that same year. The New Apostolic Reformation and the broader charismatic prophetic industry have restored the title, the platform, and the confident announcement of coming peace and prosperity, and have quietly retired the test. Failed words are re-dated, spiritualised, or blamed on the hearers' unbelief; the man who gave them keeps his conference schedule. The dictionary is cessationist and holds that the canon is closed, but the point here is one that even a consistent continuationist must feel: a movement that will not apply Deuteronomy 18 and Jeremiah 28 to its own prophets has not restored the office — it has abolished the only safeguard the office ever had. Meanwhile 1 Corinthians 14:3 stands, and its criterion is not spectacle but whether the church was built.
roots_summary: Hebrew naba' (H5012), to prophesy, to speak by inspiration; nabiy' (H5030), a prophet, a spokesman; Greek propheteuo (G4395), to speak forth God's word.
roots_lines: Hebrew naba' (H5012) — to prophesy, to speak or sing by the Spirit; used of Saul among the prophets and of Ezekiel commanded to prophesy to the bones; Ezekiel 37:4, 1 Samuel 10:11.
Hebrew nabiy' (H5030) — a prophet, a spokesman for another; Aaron is Moses' nabiy', which defines the office exactly; Exodus 7:1, Deuteronomy 18:18.
Greek propheteuo (G4395) — to speak forth the mind of God; in the epistles a gift of edification, exhortation and comfort to the assembly; 1 Corinthians 14:3-4, 14:31.
usage: “The prophet which prophesieth of peace…then shall the prophet be known” — the burden of proof on the comfortable word.
“He prophesieth of the times that are far off” — conceding the word while escaping its claim.
“He that prophesieth edifieth the church” — the New Testament measure.

pos: n. and part. (a grinding of the teeth in rage or anguish; rendering Greek brugmos and Hebrew charaq)
etymology: Middle English gnasten, of Scandinavian origin, imitative of the grinding of teeth. The Greek brugmos is likewise a sound-word: the grating of teeth.
biblical_def: The phrase “weeping and gnashing of teeth” is the Lord's own recurring description of the final state of the lost, and He uses it seven times — six in Matthew and once in Luke. It falls on the children of the kingdom cast into outer darkness (Mat 8:12); on those gathered out of the field at the end of the world and cast into the furnace of fire (Mat 13:42, 13:50); on the man without a wedding garment, bound hand and foot (Mat 22:13); on the servant cut asunder and appointed his portion with the hypocrites (Mat 24:51); on the unprofitable servant who buried his talent (Mat 25:30). Two things belong to the sound. Weeping is grief; gnashing, in its Old Testament use, is rage — the enemies of the righteous gnash upon him with their teeth (Psa 35:16; Lam 2:16), and the council gnashed on Stephen with their teeth before they stoned him (Act 7:54). Hell is therefore not portrayed as sorrowful repentance. It is grief and fury together, and unending. That the tenderest Teacher who ever spoke is the one who says it seven times is a fact the church is not at liberty to soften.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gnashing as a grinding or striking of the teeth together, as in rage, pain, or despair.
webster_full: GNASH, v.t. To strike the teeth together, as in anger or pain.
GNASH, v.i. To grind the teeth; to rage even to collision of the teeth.
GNASHING, n. A grinding or striking of the teeth in rage or anguish.
scriptures: Mat 8:12
But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
And cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
The wicked shall see it, and be grieved; he shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away: the desire of the wicked shall perish.
corruption_summary: Annihilationism and universalism both require the gnashing to stop, and both must therefore explain away the one description of hell that Christ Himself repeated most often.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of eternal conscious punishment is not built on a single proof text; it is built on the settled speech of Christ, and this phrase is its signature. Seven times He said weeping and gnashing of teeth, and He said it in the plainest didactic settings — the sermon, the parables of the kingdom, the discourse on the last things. Annihilationism, argued in the evangelical world by Edward Fudge and John Stott among others, must read the fire as consuming rather than tormenting and the gnashing as brief; universalism, in its ancient Origenist and modern forms, must read it as remedial. Both proposals founder on the same rock: the gnashing is rage, not repentance. In every Old Testament use — the enemies gnashing on the righteous in Psalm 35, the adversaries hissing and gnashing in Lamentations 2, the council gnashing on Stephen in Acts 7 — teeth are ground in fury against God or His servants. Nothing in the picture is turning toward God. The LBCF (32.2) confesses the wicked cast into eternal torments and punished with everlasting destruction, and the confession is only saying after Him what the Lord Jesus said first. The dictionary preaches the doctrine as He preached it: soberly, often, and with tears — never with relish, and never with revision.
roots_summary: Greek brugmos (G1030), a grating or gnashing of the teeth; brucho (G1031), to grind the teeth; Hebrew charaq (H2786), to grind or gnash the teeth in rage.
roots_lines: Greek brugmos (G1030) — a gnashing, a grating of the teeth; always joined to weeping and always in the Lord's own words about judgment; Matthew 8:12, 13:42, 22:13, 25:30.
Greek brucho (G1031) — to grind the teeth; used once, of the Sanhedrin against Stephen; Acts 7:54.
Hebrew charaq (H2786) — to grind or gnash the teeth in rage; the enemies of the righteous, and the wicked who melts away; Psalm 35:16, 112:10, Lamentations 2:16.
usage: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” — seven times from the lips of Christ.
“He shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away” — the rage of the wicked at the prosperity of the righteous.
“They gnashed on him with their teeth” — the council before the stoning of Stephen.

pos: v. (third person singular of cry: to call out, to appeal aloud; rendering Hebrew tsa'aq, za'aq, qara')
etymology: Old French crier, from Latin quiritare, to wail or to call upon the citizens for help. The Hebrew tsa'aq is the shriek of one under injustice, and it is a legal appeal as much as a sound.
biblical_def: The first cry in Scripture comes from the ground: “the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground” (Gen 4:10). Blood unjustly shed has a voice, and God hears it whether or not any man does — which is the foundation of every doctrine of divine justice. The law then attaches the same word to the poor man's pledge: if you take a man's garment for a pledge, restore it before sundown, “when he crieth unto me, that I will hear; for I am gracious” (Exo 22:27). God appoints Himself the hearer of the cry of the man with no advocate. So the King is described: “he shall deliver the needy when he crieth; the poor also, and him that hath no helper” (Psa 72:12). The soul of the wounded crieth out from the city, and God layeth not folly to them (Job 24:12). And the saint's cry is homesickness for God Himself: “my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God” (Psa 84:2). Finally wisdom cries: “Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets” (Pro 1:20) — God is not silent, and men perish under a preaching they have heard.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to cry as to utter a loud voice; to call importunately; to implore; to exclaim in distress or supplication; and, of a herald, to proclaim.
webster_full: CRY, v.i. To utter a loud voice; to speak, call or exclaim with vehemence.
2. To call importunately; to utter a loud voice, with earnestness; to implore; to supplicate.
3. To utter a loud voice in weeping; to lament; to shed tears with audible sound.
scriptures: Gen 4:10
And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground.
For he shall deliver the needy when he crieth; the poor also, and him that hath no helper.
Pro 1:20
Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets:
corruption_summary: The cry of the oppressed has been annexed to political programmes as an autonomous claim, and detached from the God who alone said He would hear it.
corruption_paragraphs: The Bible is emphatic that God hears the cry of the poor, the widow, the fatherless, the stranger, and the man whose blood is in the ground, and it never treats that cry as a small matter. Exodus 22:27 puts the divine character behind it: when he crieth unto me, I will hear; for I am gracious. What has happened in modern usage is not that the cry has been amplified but that it has been detached. The categories of Scripture — the poor, the afflicted, the oppressed, the widow, the orphan — are covenantal categories under a God who judges, and the cry is addressed to Him; that is what makes it a claim rather than a grievance. Reassigned to a purely political frame, the cry becomes a bare demand backed by whatever power can be mustered, and it loses two things immediately: the certainty of being heard, and the standard by which a just remedy could be recognised. The church must not answer this by growing cold toward the cry, which would be a graver error than the one it corrects; Proverbs 21:13 warns the man who stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor that he shall cry himself and not be heard. It answers by keeping the cry addressed where Genesis 4:10 addressed it — unto me, from the ground.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsa'aq (H6817) and za'aq (H2199), to cry out for help, to shriek under oppression; qara' (H7121), to call, to proclaim; ranan (H7442), to cry aloud, as Wisdom in the street.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsa'aq (H6817) — to cry out, to call for help; the blood from the ground and Israel's cry in Egypt; Genesis 4:10, Exodus 3:7.
Hebrew za'aq (H2199) — to shriek, to cry out in distress; the recurring verb of the judges cycle, when Israel cried unto the LORD; Judges 3:9, Psalm 22:5.
Hebrew ranan (H7442) — to cry aloud, to shout for joy; Wisdom lifting her voice in the streets; Proverbs 1:20, 8:3.
usage: “The voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground” — the first cry, and the ground of all divine justice.
“When he crieth unto me, that I will hear; for I am gracious” — God as the hearer of the man with no advocate.
“Wisdom crieth without” — God is not silent; men perish under a preaching they have heard.

pos: v. (past tense of lie: to speak falsehood with intent to deceive; rendering Hebrew kazab and kachash, Greek pseudomai)
etymology: Old English leogan, to lie. The Hebrew kazab means to fail or be found false, as a brook that dries in summer; the Greek pseudomai gives English pseudo-.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version records the sin in ascending seriousness. An old prophet in Bethel stops a man of God on the road and claims an angelic revision of his orders — “But he lied unto him” (1Ki 13:18) — and the younger man, who had withstood a king, is destroyed by a lie from a fellow prophet. Asaph records the nation's religion: “they did flatter him with their mouth, and they lied unto him with their tongues” (Psa 78:36), lying to God in the very act of worship. Isaiah presses the cause: “of whom hast thou been afraid or feared, that thou hast lied, and hast not remembered me?” (Isa 57:11) — the fear of man is the engine of falsehood, and forgetting God is what makes it possible. Then Ananias in the church, and Peter's word: “thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God” (Act 5:4). That sentence is the doctrine of the whole subject. Every lie is told in the hearing of God, and it is finally told to Him. Lying is not merely socially corrosive; it is a direct assault on the character of the God who cannot lie, and Revelation twice puts liars outside the city with sorcerers and murderers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to lie as to utter falsehood with an intention to deceive, or with an immoral design; and lied as the past tense, having uttered such falsehood.
webster_full: LIE, v.i. To utter falsehood with an intention to deceive, or with an immoral design.
Thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God.
LIED, pret. of lie. Uttered falsehood with intent to deceive.
scriptures: He said unto him, I am a prophet also as thou art; and an angel spake unto me by the word of the LORD, saying, Bring him back with thee into thine house, that he may eat bread and drink water. But he lied unto him.
Nevertheless they did flatter him with their mouth, and they lied unto him with their tongues.
And of whom hast thou been afraid or feared, that thou hast lied, and hast not remembered me, nor laid it to thy heart? have not I held my peace even of old, and thou fearest me not?
corruption_summary: The lie has been reclassified as a social lubricant — the harmless untruth, the necessary exaggeration, the curated self — and the biblical account of it as an assault on God's own nature has been quietly filed away.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter's sentence to Ananias is the doctrine in nine words: thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God. Ananias had told a manageable lie about a manageable sum in a voluntary offering, and by any ordinary reckoning it was a small deceit inside a generous act. Scripture reckons otherwise, because the audience of every lie is God. Modern moral vocabulary has almost no room left for this. Untruth is graded by its social consequences — the white lie, the harmless exaggeration, the professionally necessary spin, the presented self that everyone knows is edited — and where consequences are small, guilt is assumed to be small. But Titus 1:2 grounds our hope in a God that cannot lie, and Revelation 21:8 and 22:15 place liars outside the city in company that startles every reader. The reason the sin is treated so gravely is that it is a direct contradiction of the divine character in the creature made to image it. Isaiah 57:11 supplies the usual cause and it is worth self-examination: of whom hast thou been afraid? Almost every lie a Christian tells can be traced to a fear of some man, and the cure is the fear of God, which drives out the other.
roots_summary: Hebrew kazab (H3576), to lie, to fail as a deceitful brook; kachash (H3584), to deceive, deny, or dissemble; Greek pseudomai (G5574), to speak falsely.
roots_lines: Hebrew kazab (H3576) — to lie, to prove false; the noun is used of a brook whose waters fail in the heat; 1 Kings 13:18, Jeremiah 15:18.
Hebrew kachash (H3584) — to deceive, to deny, to feign submission; Isaiah's charge against the idolatrous nation; Isaiah 57:11, Joshua 7:11.
Greek pseudomai (G5574) — to speak falsely, to lie; Peter's word to Ananias, and Paul's command that the new man lie not one to another; Acts 5:4, Colossians 3:9.
usage: “But he lied unto him” — a prophet destroyed by a prophet's falsehood.
“They lied unto him with their tongues” — lying to God in the act of worship.
“Thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God” — the audience of every lie.

pos: v. (past tense of rehearse: to recount in order; to repeat what was said or done)
etymology: Old French rehercier, to harrow over again, from herce, a harrow — to go back over the same ground. In the Authorized Version it never means practice; it always means to recount.
biblical_def: To rehearse in the Authorized Version is to lay a matter out in order before someone who has a right to hear it. Samuel, having heard Israel's demand for a king, “rehearsed them in the ears of the LORD” (1Sa 8:21) — the prophet's first act with bad news was to take it, word for word, to God. When David's words about the Philistine were reported, “they rehearsed them before Saul” (1Sa 17:31). Then twice in Acts, at moments of decision. Challenged by the circumcision party for eating with Gentiles, “Peter rehearsed the matter from the beginning, and expounded it by order unto them” (Act 11:4) — no argument from authority, no appeal to his office; he simply laid out what God had done, in sequence, and the objection died. Returning from the first missionary journey, Paul and Barnabas gathered the church and “rehearsed all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles” (Act 14:27). The pattern is worth marking: the apostolic answer to controversy was narrative testimony, ordered and verifiable, of what God had actually done.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to rehearse as to repeat; to recite; to relate; to tell over; to recount or narrate in order.
webster_full: REHEARSE, v.t. To repeat; to recite; to utter or narrate again what has been said or written.
2. To relate; to tell; to recount; to narrate in order.
REHEARSED, pp. Repeated; recited; narrated; told over.
scriptures: And Samuel heard all the words of the people, and he rehearsed them in the ears of the LORD.
Act 11:4
But Peter rehearsed the matter from the beginning, and expounded it by order unto them, saying,
And when they were come, and had gathered the church together, they rehearsed all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles.
corruption_summary: Where Scripture rehearses what God has done, the modern report rehearses what the workers have achieved — numbers, reach, momentum — and the grammar of the sentence quietly changes the subject.
