corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has simply narrowed in ordinary English to mean practising a performance, which is a real loss but not a corruption. What is worth recovering is the discipline the biblical usage describes. Acts 14:27 gives the apostolic missionary report in a single sentence, and every noun in it belongs to God: they rehearsed all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles. Compare the ordinary shape of a modern ministry report, in which the subject of the sentences is generally the ministry — what we launched, what we reached, what we grew — with God appearing in a clause of thanks at the end. The difference is not modesty; it is theology. Peter in Acts 11:4 faced a genuine church crisis and answered it by rehearsing the matter from the beginning and expounding it by order, and the record says his hearers held their peace and glorified God. A church would be strengthened by recovering both halves of that practice: bad news carried first into the ears of the LORD, as Samuel carried it, and good news reported with God as the subject of the verbs.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar (H1696), to speak, to declare; Greek ektithemi (G1620), to set forth in order, to expound; Greek anangello (G312), to report, to declare fully.
roots_lines: Hebrew dabar (H1696) — to speak, to declare, to recount; Samuel repeating Israel's words in the ears of the LORD; 1 Samuel 8:21.
Greek ektithemi (G1620) — to set out, to expound in order; Peter's orderly account at Jerusalem and Priscilla and Aquila expounding the way to Apollos; Acts 11:4, 18:26.
Greek anangello (G312) — to report, to declare fully what has been seen; the missionary report at Antioch; Acts 14:27, 15:4.
usage: “He rehearsed them in the ears of the LORD” — bad news carried first to God.
“Peter rehearsed the matter from the beginning, and expounded it by order” — controversy answered with ordered testimony.
“Rehearsed all that God had done with them” — the missionary report with God as the subject.

pos: v. (past tense of confer: to consult together; to take counsel with; rendering Greek sumballo and prosanatithemi)
etymology: Latin conferre, from con-, together, and ferre, to bring — to bring together, whether counsel or a gift. The Authorized Version uses the older sense of consulting.
biblical_def: The word marks four consultations, and their objects tell the story. Adonijah, setting up to be king, “conferred with Joab the son of Zeruiah, and with Abiathar the priest” (1Ki 1:7) — a general and a priest recruited for a usurpation, and both men ended badly. The Sanhedrin, unable to deny the miracle done on the lame man, “conferred among themselves” (Act 4:15) — a council conferring about how to suppress a fact it could not refute. Festus “conferred with the council” and answered Paul, Unto Caesar shalt thou go (Act 25:12) — ordinary lawful procedure, by which God moved His apostle to Rome. And Paul: when it pleased God to reveal His Son in him, “immediately I conferred not with flesh and blood” (Gal 1:16). That last is the hinge of Galatians. Paul's gospel did not come by consultation, negotiation, or committee; he received it by revelation of Jesus Christ, and the point matters because the Galatian troublers were arguing that Paul's message was a second-hand and softened version of Jerusalem's. Counsel is a good thing — in the multitude of counsellors there is safety — but the gospel itself is not a thing men confer about. It is received and then declared.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to confer as to converse; to consult together, implying conversation on some serious or important subject; and transitively, to give or bestow.
webster_full: CONFER, v.i. To discourse; to converse; to consult together; implying conversation on some serious or important subject.
CONFER, v.t. To give or bestow; followed by on.
CONFERRED, pp. Consulted with; also, given; bestowed.
scriptures: And he conferred with Joab the son of Zeruiah, and with Abiathar the priest: and they following Adonijah helped him.
Act 4:15
But when they had commanded them to go aside out of the council, they conferred among themselves,
Gal 1:16
To reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the heathen; immediately I conferred not with flesh and blood:
corruption_summary: The gospel is increasingly treated as a proposal to be negotiated with the surrounding culture, which is precisely the conferring with flesh and blood Paul refused.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 1:16 is a deliberately provocative sentence, and Paul meant it to be. He had just been given the revelation on which his whole apostolate rested, and his first act was not to consult — not Jerusalem, not the apostles before him, not the men whose approval would have made his position comfortable. He went into Arabia. The reason is given in the verses around it: the gospel he preached is not after man, neither received of man, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ. A message received by revelation may be tested against Scripture, and Paul submits to that test constantly; it may not be adjusted by consultation. The modern corruption is a settled habit of conferring, in which the church takes the surrounding culture as a party to the negotiation and asks which clauses can be modified to keep the relationship. It is done with the best of motives and always in the name of reaching people. But a gospel arrived at by conferring with flesh and blood is by definition after man, and Paul has already pronounced on it in verse 8: though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you, let him be accursed. The proper place for conferring is everywhere else. Paul who would not confer about the gospel took Barnabas, took counsel at Jerusalem about a practical question, and told the Corinthians to judge what he said.
roots_summary: Greek sumballo (G4820), to throw together, to confer or consider; prosanatithemi (G4323), to lay a matter before another for counsel; Hebrew idiom dabar 'im, to have words with, to consult.
roots_lines: Greek sumballo (G4820) — to throw or bring together, to confer, to ponder; the Sanhedrin conferring, and Mary pondering these things in her heart; Acts 4:15, Luke 2:19.
Greek prosanatithemi (G4323) — to lay a matter before someone for their judgment; used only in Galatians, of what Paul refused to do; Galatians 1:16, 2:6.
Hebrew dabar 'im — to speak with, to have words with, and so to consult; Adonijah's recruitment of Joab and Abiathar; 1 Kings 1:7.
usage: “He conferred with Joab…and with Abiathar the priest” — a usurpation assembled by consultation.
“They conferred among themselves” — a council deliberating how to suppress a fact it could not deny.
“Immediately I conferred not with flesh and blood” — the gospel received, not negotiated.

pos: n. (the act of setting one thing beside another to judge its worth; also a parable or similitude; rendering Greek parabole)
etymology: Latin comparatio, from comparare, to pair or match, from par, equal. To compare is to set two things side by side as if they were of one kind — which is why comparison is so often a lie.
biblical_def: Gideon uses comparison to disarm a quarrel. The men of Ephraim chided with him sharply, and he answered, “What have I done now in comparison of you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?” (Jdg 8:2), and again, “what was I able to do in comparison of you?” (Jdg 8:3) — and their anger was abated when he had said that. A soft answer, made of a deliberate comparison in his brethren's favour, turned away wrath that a defence of his own record would have inflamed. Haggai uses comparison to expose grief: to the old men who had seen the first house, the second was “in your eyes in comparison of it as nothing” (Hag 2:3) — and the LORD does not deny the comparison; He answers it with a promise that the glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former. Then the Lord Jesus takes the word for His own method: “Whereunto shall we liken the kingdom of God? or with what comparison shall we compare it?” (Mar 4:30), and the Greek is parabole, a parable. Comparison rightly used is how the unseen kingdom is taught to earthbound men, by a mustard seed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines comparison as the act of comparing; the consideration of two or more objects with a view to discover their agreement or difference; also a simile or similitude used in argument.
webster_full: COMPARISON, n. The act of comparing; the act of considering the relation between two persons or things, when opposed to each other.
2. The state of being compared; comparative estimate; proportion.
3. A simile, similitude, or illustration by similitude; as, a comparison used in argument.
scriptures: Jdg 8:2
And he said unto them, What have I done now in comparison of you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?
Hag 2:3
Who is left among you that saw this house in her first glory? and how do ye see it now? is it not in your eyes in comparison of it as nothing?
Mar 4:30
And he said, Whereunto shall we liken the kingdom of God? or with what comparison shall we compare it?
corruption_summary: A technology of continuous comparison now runs in every pocket, and the covetousness it manufactures is treated as an inevitable feature of life rather than as the sin the tenth commandment names.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul names the practice and its result in one verse: they that measure themselves by themselves, and compare themselves among themselves, are not wise (2Co 10:12). The comparison is unwise because the standard is wrong — it substitutes other men for God — and because it is rigged: a man compares his known interior to another man's presented exterior and reaches a verdict on both. Our age has industrialised this. The ordinary condition of a person with a telephone is a continual, involuntary comparison of his ordinary life with an edited highlight of ten thousand others, and the two commonest fruits are exactly the two Scripture warns of: covetousness, which is idolatry, and the despair of the man who concludes he is nothing. Haggai 2:3 shows God's dealing with the second. He does not tell the old men that their comparison was false — the second house genuinely was as nothing beside Solomon's — He tells them to be strong and work, for I am with you, and promises a greater glory to that very house, which was fulfilled when the Desire of all nations walked in its courts. The cure for a wrong comparison is not a flattering one. It is a true one, made against the right standard, with a promise attached.
roots_summary: Greek parabole (G3850), a parable, proverb, or comparison; sugkrino (G4793), to compare one thing with another; Hebrew idiom “in comparison of” rendering a phrase of relative worth.
roots_lines: Greek parabole (G3850) — literally a throwing alongside; a comparison, similitude, or parable; the Lord's chosen instrument for teaching the kingdom; Mark 4:30, Matthew 13:3.

Greek sugkrino (G4793) — to compare, to judge one thing by another; Paul's word for comparing spiritual things with spiritual, and for the unwise comparison of self with self; 1 Corinthians 2:13, 2 Corinthians 10:12.
Hebrew idiom of Judges 8:2 — a phrase of relative worth, “what am I beside you”; Gideon's soft answer that turned away Ephraim's wrath; Judges 8:2-3.
usage: “What have I done now in comparison of you?” — a soft answer built out of a comparison in his brethren's favour.
“In your eyes in comparison of it as nothing” — the old men weeping at the second house.
“With what comparison shall we compare it?” — the kingdom taught by a mustard seed.
